KO.rationale: KO is an elite franchise — 40.4% ROE, 25.9% net margin, 61.4% gross margin, asset-light concentrate model, 64-year dividend streak, dominant CSD share (~46-47%). However, the stock is priced for near-perfection at 29.2x trailing P/E (97th percentile of 1-year range), 11.8x P/B (92nd percentile), and a 3.4% earnings yield that sits 114bps below the 10-year Treasury yield of 4.54%. The P/E has expanded ~23% from its trough of 23.7x while net margin and ROE have been flat at 0.259 and 0.404 respectively — pure multiple expansion, not earnings improvement. The stock has rallied ~25% in three quarters ($66.10 to $82.63) with no fundamental acceleration to justify it. On a forward basis, consensus FY2026 EPS of ~$3.26 implies ~25x forward P/E, which is still a premium for a mid-single-digit grower. The IRS transfer-pricing dispute poses a potential $14B additional liability (oral arguments began June 2026), Mexico's 2026 excise tax is a regional headwind, and the strong dollar (120.75) pressures international revenue. Q2 2026 earnings on July 28 could be a catalyst, but with consensus expecting only 5-7% EPS growth and the stock near all-time highs, the bar for positive surprise is high while the downside from any miss is amplified by the stretched multiple. Berkshire's repositioning away from KO as a top holding is a soft signal on relative attractiveness. The business is excellent; the price has already captured that and then some. Risk/reward is asymmetrically skewed to the downside at this valuation.

Bearish analysts highlight Latin America as a relative weak spot… the planned 2026 excise tax in Mexico could weigh on consumption and limit pricing power.
